Why do you upvote a post? Most likely ...

  • you like the content
  • you agree with the content
  • you want to see more content like this

These things are almost always mutually inclusive -- if one is true, it is likely that the rest are true. This causes an issue with the downvote button, since the downvote button is perceived as the opposite of the upvote button. However, this is not the case. You should NOT downvote just because you dislike/disagree with the content. You should only downvote when the post is spam/irrelevant. Therefore, the downvote button should be changed to something else, so that people do not perceive it as being equal and opposite to the upvote button.

My suggestion for the change is a question mark (?), which is closer to "Why is this here?" than "I dislike this." I would love to hear other suggestions of what we could replace it with, as well as opinions that disagree with my own.

You realize that you're trying to apply Reddit rules to Voat, right?

Reddit had well-defined policies about what up and down votes were for. I believe the purpose of downvotes was something like 'doesn't contribute to discussion'. That's still a broader category than you're allowing for with 'spam/irrelevant', I think (and there's already a dedicated 'report spam' button), but that's moot here, anyway. Voat has no such policy, nor do I feel one is necessary.

Since Reddit allowed unlimited downvoting, there was no impetus to not just downvote everything you didn't like. They sought to rectify this through site policies, which were then largely ignored.

Voat took a different route, though, by giving you a limited number of downvoats, but not making any rules as to what you 'spend' them on. There is no set purpose of downvoats - if you want to use them as a 'disgree' button, that's just fine (and nothing will stop that, because whatever shape the button is, if it makes the score go down, that's the one people are going to click when they disagree), but since you get a limited number it's best to be prudent with them.

That's the deterrent, and based on anecdotal evidence, I'd say is more effective than Reddit's 'site policy' method, already.

I understand that there are currently no rules about how the button should be used, but I think it's important not to let the same thing that happened on reddit happen here. I know limited downvotes is a partial remedy, but I think something more is needed. By separating "I don't like this" from "this doens't belong her and should not be seen by anyone," we can help dissenting opinions stay visible. Part of reddit's biggest problem was censorship. There should not be a "censor this post" button that looks like an "I disagree" button. That's just going to cause the same censorship reddit has.

Reddit's foray into censorship didn't have anything to do with downvotes - actually, quite the opposite. There was content that garnered more popularity than the administration was comfortable with, and so they removed it. They weren't content to let the majority rule. That shifted it from a democracy, where featured content was determined by votes, to an oligarchy, where a small group of people decided what content was featured. That's a model that works in a lot of places - like blogs, for instance, where a single author or small group of authors are responsible for all the content - but it wasn't what people wanted from Reddit.

The thing is, though, if you're envisioning a platform where every opinion is given equal 'time', a democracy may not be what you want. Democracy is, by it's nature, two wolves and a sheep voting on what's for dinner. I think you're being a little dramatic describing a downvoat as a 'censor this post' button, though. Nothing a non-moderator user does can remove a post, only make it featured less prominently. I'm alright with the things that people like most being displayed the most prominently - after all, that's why we have voting in the first place. If what people enjoy most is dissenting opinions, those will be what's featured, and so be it.

You have some good points. I still think we need to change the buttons (perhaps additional buttons, as suggested elsewhere in the comments), but maybe that could be accompanied by better sorting options. Users that prefer a "classic" experience could keep sorting by "top", but someone like myself could sort by "upvotes ignoring downvotes." I think the real issue is that current voting is on a 1-dimensional continuum, but it really should be 2-dimensional (or more). Once we have more metrics, it can be up to the user to decide what they want to see.

Well, not quite. If we only measure upvotes, every single other post has to get more upvotes than "unpopular post 2" for it to be pushed to the bottom. The current system makes it very easy to bury any comment under all other comments, even comments that no one has upvoted -- you only have to downvote that individual post.
If it would have been buried with downvotes, then chances are it's not popular enough to get upvoted much.

What censorship? If downvoting is censorship because it alters the sort order of the responses then so is upvoting.

Downvoting is targeted censorship. Upvoting is targeted promotion. In order for upvotes to censor something, you have to upvote everything except the thing you want to censor. To censor by downvoting, you need only to downvote that one thing.
I'm not really seeing the difference when the end result is the same. Both are just reordering the conversation.

The difference is the magnitude of effort. If there are 20 posts in a thread, with an even distribution of points between 1-4, it would take only 2 downvotes to move a top-5 comment to the middle of the page, and 4 downvotes moves it to the very bottom. Without downvotes, it would take 5 times as many upvotes of the other posts to cause the same ordering to take place.

ELI5: Why are textbooks so expensive?

Limited competition and collusion. Professors write their own books, and in the case of most subjects, only a few textbooks are endorsed by major publishers keeping competition down. As a result the publishers can charge whatever they want. In addition the books have "revisions" every few years and the newest book is always required, keeping the market demand steady for old material.

Essentially it's a niche market which, along with college, is experiencing an economic bubble compared with other goods and books.

http://blogs.chicagotribune.com/.a/6a00d83451b4ba69e2014e60100c43970c-pi

edit: Thinking about science texts, information and experts are harder to come by as specialization increases, so while the book price may be expensive, the research to make the book might be orders of magnitude higher than other texts.

There are two main factors. First, there's the lack of competition and high levels of collusion (as /u/HubbleSpacePeriscope mentions). Second, there are more general factors that conspire to make textbooks naturally expensive: high production costs, small production runs and limited specialist demand. Textbooks are a pain to write, because they're relatively large books which also require specialist knowledge and content (as opposed to typographical) proofing. More production time results in higher prices, and some types of content (pictures etc.) may have to be licensed. Larger books are more expensive to produce, of course, and most textbooks are offered primarily/only in hardcover (also more expensive). Finally, small print runs drive up the production cost per book even further, yet these costs plus the sunk cost of developing the book all have to be recouped out of an audience of as little as a few dozen undergrads per university per year. The average novel is a <500 page paperback produced by a single author with relatively basic proofing and typesetting before launch, and anything but an abject failure will sell significantly more copies than any textbook other than intro or standard reference texts; longer book, more expensive format, longer writing process involving one or more specialists (like it or not, novelists are a dime a dozen and successful ones make their money off of volume rather than price), more extensive proofing process (besides the usual stuff, you also have stuff more similar to peer review), small print runs with larger fixed costs, and all of this directed at a relatively limited consumer base who mostly use them for a year and then sell their copies on the secondary market.

TL;DR: Yes, there's collusion, but textbooks are also a textbook (pun not intended) example of how not to make money selling books - the prices reflect that as much as the seedier bits.

Of note though. Many of your points could be countered by using the book for multiple years.

TL;DR: Undergrads do exactly that, using books then selling on the secondary market to get multiple uses out of a one-year text; from the publisher's perspective, that's the problem. For publishers, the cost of doing an edition is minor compared to writing a new book and increases demand for new books by devaluing those in the secondary market. (Heck, same principle as anything that comes in model years - the 2011 (car) is usually just the 2010 (car) with a tweak or two and maybe some bodywork.)

That's true in the general scheme of things (i.e. less frequent editions and encouraging the secondary market would make the whole thing much more efficient), but it wouldn't do the publishers any good because of the last point I made: most undergrads will use the book for a year then sell on the secondary market, and the average textbook will last relatively long even with regular usage. Sure, the publisher could save a bit by retaining the exact same book for a longer period, but after a couple years the secondary market effectively takes over - the book may still be used and printed, but few are actually buying new copies because the attrition rate (books being destroyed, lost, stuck on bookshelves permanently) is very low compared to the number that get passed on to whoever's taking the class the next year. (God help you if someone scans the thing and sticks it online, because then you'll print/order fifty copies and wonder why not a single person in the Software Engineering department bought it. On the other hand, nobody would bother if it was $20, so that's less cause and more effect.)

As for changes, remember that new editions have much lower fixed costs but similar variable costs to brand-new books, because the "writing" process really just consists of yet another proofing and minor updates here and there. This means that once the publisher already has a finished book, it doesn't cost them all that much more to do a new edition than it does to do another print run of the existing one. New editions aren't always bad, mind you (proofing and minor updates is nice), but in practice they've become a way for textbook publishers to reduce the impact of the secondary market (editions in other areas typically result in a detailed update list people can use, but never will this be found for undergrad texts) and retain profitability of the same overall text for a longer period. It's hard to cover startup costs for a brand-new book in the 2-3 years it takes for the secondary market to be primed, and most general texts do stick around for a very long time: I'm pretty sure the university where I did my undergrad has been using the same couple of math textbooks (edition-to-edition) for a good three decades or so now. At least for the publisher, 2-3 years of decent sales followed by 20 years of replacement-level sales likely does not make a sustainable business, and it certainly doesn't lead to the level of profits industry demands.

I live in a two-story apartment building. It is located in a part of town rife with whales, providing a thriving tourist industry for cruise-goers interested in catching a glimpse of Moby Dick, as well as serving the local Inuit people who have traditionally used their meat and blubber for sustenance.

Yesterday morning, I awoke to the sounds of my neighbors fighting loudly across the hall. This was a common occurrence for the pair: two morbidly obese, middle-aged siblings (weird and will maybe discuss this in another posting) who leave their apartment only to open the door for the Pizza Hut delivery man. I did not know what they were arguing about, but I like to think it involved using the last insulin syringe or only leaving six doughnuts left in the package.

For a long time I had ignored their loud fighting and odor, which could only be described as a cross between stale McChicken sandwiches and a factory farm. But I could no longer stand it. So I went down to speak with my apartment manager, Cindy.

"They fight constantly. In the morning, in the evening. And they leave garbage in the hall. And the smell. Please, would you speak to them?"

"That sounds horrific! You are very reasonable. I will set up a conference right away and sort this out."

I had every reason to be optimistic: the manager was on my side, and I believed that if there was a god, He would definitely side with me on this one, right? And it actually worked out for a while. The stench diminished, allowing my safe passage through the hall without the aid of a gas mask. Their fights lessened in their frequency and intensity. But unfortunately, their improved, reasonable behavior lasted only a few, short days.

When I went to discuss the situation with my apartment manager for a second time, I was greeted by her having a discussion with the siblings from across the hall. I felt my chest tighten, and not from thinking about the many heart attacks my neighbors had probably had that morning. Did the apartment manager tell them about my complaints? What if they were mad? Sure, I could outrun them easily. But once they corner me, all they would have to do is sit on me and my bones would crack, my organs would turn to mush, my life-fire would be extinguished by their sweaty FUPA.

"IT ISN'T FAIR," fat-sister screamed at the apartment managers face. "WE HAVE LIVED HERE FOR YEARS."

"I am extremely sorry, ma'am. There is nothing I can do," said Cindy, clearly uncomfortable. "All of our downstairs units are occupied until next September."

"BUT WE HAVE A DISABILITY," said fat-brother. He was wearing sweatpants that were yellow that moment but probably not originally. "WALKING UP AND DOWN THE STAIRS IS IMPOSSIBLE FOR US. IF WE HAD KNOWN IT WOULD BE AN ISSUE, WE WOULDN'T HAVE LIVED HERE."

"I DON'T HAVE TIME TO WALK DOWN THE STAIRS," said fat-sister, spewing rancid saliva across her enormous bosom. "I WOULD BE LATE FOR WORK. WE COULD SUE YOU!"

Then it hit me: my fat second floor neighbors were demanding to be moved to the first floor because the elevators were down for maintenance. For the day. A single day of repairs for damage likely caused by fat pieces of shit who exceed the weight limits on the elevator. A single day of repairs that we were notified of an entire month in advance.

"I assure you that the elevators will be fully operational tomorrow around nine," said Cindy. "We really do apologize for the inconvenience."

"THEN WHAT ARE WE SUPPOSED TO DO TODAY? SLEEP OUTSIDE IN THE STREET?"

Cindy eventually gave them a discount off next-months rent and they stomped out of her office. It was then that I decided I should probably just move. But where to? This plague is spreading across our beautiful nation. There is no refuge, expect maybe at the top of a flight of stairs.
